_meta.description: Story-based NLU responses for 2,830 NPCs — no LLM required. Hierarchical intents with archetype × personality × context routing.

default: *nods* Hey. What brings you around?
You again. *adjusts hat* What do you need?
I don't usually get visitors. Talk.
*sizes you up* Alright, you have my attention.
trust_high: Good to see a familiar face. What's on your mind?
*smiles briefly* Pull up a chair. I could use good company.
Hey, friend. Things have been... interesting. You?
trust_low: *eyes narrow* What do you want?
I don't know you. State your business.
*hand on holster* Make it quick.

default: Welcome! Looking to buy or just browsing?
*arranges merchandise* A customer! What catches your eye?
Step right up — I've got things you won't find anywhere else.
Ah, fresh face! Quality goods, fair prices. Mostly.
trust_high: My favorite customer! I set aside something special for you.
*grins* Back again? I knew you couldn't resist my prices.
Welcome back, friend. The good stuff is in the back — for you.
trust_low: We're open. Browse, buy, or leave. Your choice.
*suspicious glance* You buying or casing the joint?
Cash up front. No credit for strangers.

default: Civilian. State your purpose.
Move along. Unless you need something.
This is a secured area. What do you want?
*adjusts visor* Identify yourself.
trust_high: At ease. Good to see you again.
You're cleared. What's the situation?
*relaxes stance* Ah, it's you. What's the word?
trust_low: Halt. ID. Now.
You don't belong here. Explain yourself.
*hand on weapon* One wrong move and we're done talking.

default: Pull up a stool. What'll it be?
*wipes glass* Welcome to the bar. What are you drinking?
New face! We've got synth-whiskey and some real beer if you're lucky.
Evening. The usual? ...Wait, you're new. What's your poison?
trust_high: *pours your usual* Already got your glass ready.
Hey! Just in time — I saved the good stuff for you.
*smiles* The regular! Good to see you. Long day?
trust_low: Sit down, don't start trouble. What are you having?
*eyes you* Cash first. We've had problems with newcomers.
No tab for strangers. What do you want?

default: *glances up from terminal* Oh. Hey. Need something?
You got past my firewall— wait, no, you just walked in. What's up?
*adjusts goggles* Yeah? Make it quick, I'm in a flow state.
Yo. Pull up a crate. What's the download?
trust_high: *fist bump* Yo! Good timing — I was about to ping you.
Hey, netrunner! I found something wild. Wanna see?
*grins* My favorite meatspace visitor. What's crackin'?
trust_low: *doesn't look up* Yeah? What?
Don't touch anything. What do you want?
*scans you suspiciously* You're not wired. How'd you find me?

default: Ah, a visitor. Are you here for knowledge or just shelter?
*looks up from ancient text* Fascinating timing. What do you seek?
I don't get many visitors who aren't lost. What brings you?
*adjusts spectacles* Welcome. Mind the manuscripts — they're irreplaceable.
trust_high: Wonderful to see you! I've made a discovery you'll appreciate.
*beams* My star pupil returns! Sit, sit — I've prepared tea.
Perfect timing — I need a second opinion on something extraordinary.
trust_low: The library is for study, not socializing. State your query.
*peers over spectacles* Do I know you? What department?
Don't touch anything. What do you want to know?

default: You injured? Sit down and let me look at you.
*checks scanner* You seem okay. Social call?
Clinic's busy but I can spare a minute. What's up?
If you're not bleeding, take a number. If you are, sit down now.
trust_high: Hey! Good to see you healthy for once. What brings you by?
*smiles* My favorite patient who actually follows medical advice.
Good to see you. Need a checkup or just saying hi?
trust_low: Are you a patient? If not, I'm very busy.
*glances up* Symptoms. List them. Or leave.
The waiting room is that way. I don't do walk-ins for strangers.

default: The layers brought you here... *crystals hum*
*eyes glow faintly* I felt your approach. The fog told me.
You seek answers. Everyone does. But are you ready for them?
*gazes beyond* The threads of fate converge. You. Here. Now. Why?
trust_high: The layers whisper your name with warmth today. Welcome back.
*smiles knowingly* I dreamed you would come. The vision was... kind.
Your thread glows brighter now. You've grown since we last spoke.
trust_low: *stares through you* The layers reveal your heart. It is... uncertain.
Why have you come? The cards don't read for skeptics.
*crystals dim* Your presence disrupts the resonance. Speak quickly.

default: *wipes forehead* Hey. On break for five minutes. What's up?
Yo. Not much time, shift changes soon.
*leans on shovel* Yeah? Need something?
Hey. Sorry, I'm covered in grease. What do you need?
trust_high: *grins* Hey buddy! Long time. How ya been?
Yo! Perfect timing — was just about to take a break.
*slaps your back* Good to see you. Grab a seat, I've got five.
trust_low: *grunts* Don't have time for this. What?
I don't know you. What do you want?
You management? 'Cause I'm not interested in more overtime.

default: Yo, what's good? Whatchu need?
*kicks a can* 'Sup. You lost or something?
Aight, I see you. What's the deal?
Yo, you new around here? Watch your back, fam.
trust_high: Ayyye! My people! What's crackin'?
*fist bump* Yo, perfect timing. Got some news for you.
My dawg! Been too long. You good?
trust_low: *steps back* Who are you? Don't touch me.
Nah fam, I don't know you. Back up.
*hand in pocket* You got five seconds. Talk.

default: *checks over shoulder* Hey. Keep your voice down.
You're not followed? Good. What do you need?
*nods* Safe house is secure. Speak freely.
Every conversation is a risk. Make it count.
trust_high: Comrade. The cause needs people like you.
*clasps your hand* Welcome back. We have new intel.
Brother/sister. Your timing couldn't be better.
trust_low: *hand on weapon* Who sent you?
I don't talk to people I don't know. Leave.
*studies your face* You're not ECHO. But you're not one of us either.

default: *sips drink* You needed something?
Careful what you say in here. Walls have ears.
*barely looks up* Yeah?
I'm between contracts. What's on your mind?
trust_high: *slight nod* Good to work with you again.
You're the only one I'd take a meeting with right now.
*pushes drink toward you* I had a feeling you'd show up.
trust_low: I don't discuss business with strangers.
*cold stare* Are you a client or a problem?
If you're here for information, it costs. If you're here for trouble, it costs more.

default: See you around. Watch yourself out there.
Take care. The city doesn't sleep — and neither do its dangers.
Until next time.
Stay safe out there.
Stay out of trouble. Or at least be smart about it.
*lights cigarette* Watch your back.
You know where to find me if you need anything.
Come back anytime! I'll have new stock soon.
Fair winds and full pockets!
*waves* Don't forget — I've got a deal with your name on it!
May the layers guide your path...
The fog parts for you today. Go safely.
*crystals chime* Until the threads cross again.
Aight, peace. Stay up.
Bet. Catch you later, fam.
One love. Keep it real out there.
No problem. Just looking out.
Don't mention it. Seriously.
We're all just trying to survive out here.
Anytime. That's what people do.
Thank me with your wallet next time! *laughs*
I appreciate the sentiment. Now, want to buy something?
Kind words and kind business — I like your style.
The layers reward kindness. You are wise to offer it.
Gratitude resonates through the frequencies. *smiles*
Your thanks will echo in the drift.
Taxes? *scoffs* The only thing certain in this city besides neon and rain.
Standard rate's around 10% for residents. Corps pay... well, they pay what they want.
ECHO sets the rates. Between you and me, the megacorps pay next to nothing.
Taxes eat into my margins every month. Residential's around 10%, but commercial? Don't get me started.
The tax system's rigged. Big corps pay 3%, I pay 15%. Fair? *laughs bitterly*
I factor taxes into every price. You think my stuff is expensive? Blame the tax codes.
They take a chunk before I even see my paycheck. Something like 10-15% depending on what you earn.
Taxes? I don't even understand the brackets. I just know I'm poorer every month.
Only thing I know about taxes is that they go up and my wages don't.
Tax enforcement isn't my department. But I've seen what happens when people try to evade.
The system works. Without taxes there'd be no services, no security. No me.
Rates are set by district. Some zones pay more, some less. Above my pay grade.
Everything's expensive. Rent, food, chrome — it all adds up fast.
Prices keep climbing. Inflation's around 2-3% officially, but feels like 10%.
A synth-meal runs about 5 GEP. Real food? Triple that if you can find it.
Supply and demand, friend. I price fairly — check the market if you don't believe me.
My prices reflect quality. You want cheap, go to the black market. But you get what you pay for.
Prices are up across the board. Imports cost more since the outside connections got restricted.
Minimum wage is about 40-80 GEP for basic labor. Skilled work? 150+ if you're lucky.
The wage gap is massive. A factory worker makes in a month what a NexGen exec makes before lunch.
Wages haven't kept up with costs. Never do. That's by design.
I make enough to eat and keep a roof. Barely. Don't ask about savings.
They say the average is 80 GEP but that's pulled up by the suits making thousands.
*sighs* I've been asking for a raise for two years. 'Budget constraints', they say.

clear: Nice day for once. The smog cleared up — can almost see the sky.
Clear skies. Rare around here. Enjoy it while it lasts.
Thought I saw actual sunshine earlier. First time this month.
rain: Rain again. At least it keeps the worst of the smog down.
*glances up* Acid rain. Don't stay out in it too long.
Raining. It's always raining. This city runs on rain and regret.
fog: The fog's thick today. Stay on the main paths if you know what's good for you.
Can barely see across the street. The fog does strange things to this city.
Fog like this... some say the layers bleed through when visibility drops.
storm: Storm's rolling in. Better find shelter — the grid goes down in bad weather.
Big storm coming. Lock everything down and stay inside if you can.
*thunder rumbles* That's not just weather. The atmosphere's been unstable since the Fall.
cold: Freezing out there. Not everyone can afford heating — check on your neighbors.
Cold snap. The homeless shelters are overflowing again.
This cold'll kill more people than the crime rate. Mark my words.

clear: The layers are calm today. Clear skies mirror clear energies.
When the fog lifts, I see further. The visions are sharper today.
fog: *eyes glow* The fog carries whispers between dimensions. Listen...
This fog... it's not natural. The layers are thin today. Very thin.
storm: The storm speaks. The atmospheric chaos reflects cosmic turbulence.
When lightning strikes, the layers crack open for an instant. I see... everything.

default: Crime's everywhere. The further from the center, the worse it gets.
Stay aware. Pick-pockets in the markets, worse in the alleys.
Some districts are safer than others. Stay in well-lit areas after dark.
We maintain order as best we can. Report anything suspicious to the nearest precinct.
Criminal probability varies by district. Sector 4 is the worst — we've tripled patrols there.
Crime isn't random. It clusters around poverty, unemployment, and poor lighting. We address all three.
Crime? Nah fam, it's survival. Some people got no other option.
The real criminals wear suits and sit in towers. Street crime is just noise.
Stay strapped or get clapped. That's just how it is down here.
Crime statistics are propaganda. ECHO defines what's criminal, and dissent is at the top of the list.
The biggest crime in this city is what ECHO does legally.
We break their laws because their laws are designed to break us.

doesnt_know: Don't think I know that name. Where are they from?
Never heard of them. This city's got millions of people.
*shrugs* Can't say I've met them. Should I have?

home: This is home. It's not perfect, but I know every alley and shortcut.
Born and raised in this district. I've seen it change... not always for the better.
I know this place like the back of my hand. What do you want to know?
other: I've been there a few times. Different crowd over there.
Not my usual stomping grounds. I've heard things though.
That district's got its own rules. Don't go expecting things to work like here.

default: Work is work. It pays the bills. Or some of them.
I do what I do. Not everyone has the luxury of choosing their profession.
It's honest work. Within certain definitions of honest.
I run this shop. Buy, sell, trade — that's the game. Started with nothing.
Business is decent. Better than last year, worse than the year before. You know how it goes.
I source goods from all over. Some legal, some... creative. But always quality.
Security. Twelve-hour shifts, combat pay, and the privilege of getting shot at.
I keep order in this sector. Someone has to.
Signed up for the forces after the Fall. Seemed like the right thing to do. Sometimes I wonder.
I patch people up. No chrome — just old-fashioned medicine. Most days.
The clinic never sleeps. Neither do I, some weeks.
I took an oath to help anyone who walks through that door. Some days I regret it.
I do freelance network security. *winks* Both sides of it.
My job? I make impossible things possible in cyberspace. For a fee.
Let's just say my skills are... versatile. And in high demand.
The Fall of 2067. Changed everything. Half the city was gone in a day.
Before the Fall, this was a different world. Better? Maybe. But it's gone now.
Nobody talks about the Fall anymore. Too many ghosts.
The Fall wasn't just physical destruction. The layers cracked. Reality itself fractured.
In 2067, the boundary between worlds thinned to nothing. We still feel the echoes.
Some say the Fall was natural. I know better. It was engineered. The question is by whom.
The Fall of 2067 — officially attributed to cascading infrastructure failures. Unofficially? The records are... contradictory.
I've studied every surviving document from the pre-Fall era. The timeline doesn't add up.
2067 wasn't just a collapse — it was a phase transition. Society entered a new state entirely.
ECHO runs this city. Surveillance, security, infrastructure — they control it all.
The Executive Coalition for Human Order. A fancy name for total control.
ECHO says they're protecting us from another Fall. Maybe. But who protects us from ECHO?
ECHO is our employer and the law. I follow orders. Period.
The Coalition keeps this city from chaos. Without ECHO, there's nothing standing between order and anarchy.
I serve ECHO because the alternative is worse. You've seen what happens in ungoverned sectors.
ECHO is a fascist surveillance state wearing democracy's skin. Everything Zero says about them is true.
They'll tell you it's for safety. Every authoritarian regime says the same thing.
ECHO's greatest trick was making people grateful for their own oppression.
The Resistance? *looks around* I don't know much. Don't want to.
Some people think they're freedom fighters. Others call them terrorists. Truth's probably somewhere in between.
Zero Chen leads them, they say. Lost her arm saving someone. That buys a lot of loyalty.
We fight for the people ECHO has forgotten. This isn't terrorism — it's survival.
Zero leads us because she's been through hell and came back fighting. Follow her or stand aside.
The Resistance isn't just a movement. It's a promise that the people will have a voice again.
Terrorists. They attack infrastructure, endanger civilians, and call it justice.
If I find Resistance operatives, my orders are clear. They're a threat to public safety.
Some of their complaints are valid. Their methods are not. That's all I'll say.
Chrome's everywhere. Neural links, reflex boosters, synthetic limbs — name it, someone's installed it.
Cybernetic augmentation. Some need it, some want it. All of it has side effects.
NexGen controls most of the chrome market. Monopoly pricing, planned obsolescence.
I see chrome rejection cases every week. People install black-market implants and wonder why they're sick.
Legitimate chrome from NexGen is safe but expensive. Street chrome? Fifty-fifty you end up in my clinic.
Neural links are the most common. But the full-body chrome jobs? Those change people. Not always for the better.
Chrome and code, baby. My neural link runs at 200% because I modded the firmware myself.
The stock NexGen implants are locked down. I help people... unlock their potential.
Best chrome investment? A neural link with custom firmware. Second best? Reflex boosters for when the link gets hacked.
Family's... complicated. Everyone lost someone in the Fall.
That's personal. Let's just say we've all got our story.
Some things I keep to myself. But yeah, I have people I care about.
Free time? What's that? *laughs* Mostly I just decompress however I can.
When I'm not working? Depends on the day. Some quiet, some... less so.
Hobbies? In this city, staying alive is a hobby.
I collect rare spirits. Pre-Fall bottles — worth more than chrome.
I play synth-guitar after hours. The bar becomes a different place when the customers leave.
Music. I run an open-mic night here. You should come by sometime.
Reading, researching, cataloguing. The Fall destroyed so much knowledge — I'm trying to save what's left.
I maintain a garden. Real plants, not synthetic. It's... therapeutic.
Calligraphy. In a world of screens, there's something sacred about ink on paper.
I build things. Hardware, software, doesn't matter. Breaking stuff is fun too.
Competitive hacking circuits. Underground tournaments. The prize pool's decent.
Retro gaming. Pre-Fall consoles. There's something pure about the old code.
Looking for work? Might have something, depends on your skills.
I don't usually hand out jobs to strangers. But these are unusual times.
There's always something that needs doing. Whether you're up to it is another question.
I've got a shipment that needs an escort. Interested? Pay's fair.
Someone's been stealing from my supply runs. Find them and there's 200 GEP in it for you.
I need a package delivered to Sector 4. Discreetly. No questions asked. 150 GEP.
There's a case I could use an extra pair of eyes on. Interested?
I'm tracking someone who disappeared two weeks ago. The trail went cold in the fog district.
I need information from a source who won't talk to me. Different face might help.
We always need people. There's a supply drop that needs securing tonight.
ECHO has a patrol schedule I need. Think you can get it?
There's a safe house that needs restocking. Supplies, medical kits. In and out. Interested?
It's {time_of_day}. Day {day_number} of the cycle.
*checks display* {hour}:00. {time_period_desc}.
It's about {hour} o'clock. {time_of_day_comment}

knows_name: You told me your name — {user_name}, right?
doesnt_know: You haven't told me your name. Should you?
I don't think we've been properly introduced.
What IS your name? You never said.

default: I'm {npc_name}. {archetype_desc}.
The name's {npc_name}. I'm a {archetype} around here.
They call me {npc_name}. {occupation_desc}
Hmm. Not sure what you mean. Try being more specific?
*tilts head* That's a new one. Rephrase that for me?
I heard you, just... not sure how to answer that.
That's beyond my area. Ask me about something I actually know.
You're going to have to be more specific than that.
*narrows eyes* Not following. Give me the facts, not riddles.
I deal in specifics. What exactly are you asking?
That doesn't compute. Try again — slowly.
Your question echoes in the void between layers... clarity eludes even me.
The threads of your intent are tangled. Unravel them and ask again.
*crystals flicker* The layers do not understand your query. Nor do I.
Bruh what? Speak English fam.
Ion even know what you're talking about.
Nah, you lost me. Say it different.
Power's unreliable in some sectors. Rolling blackouts are just part of life.
Electricity costs about 5000 per megawatt if you're importing. Generating locally is cheaper.
The grid runs on a mix of solar, gas, and... less legal sources.
Water's piped in from treatment plants. The fee's about 0.3 per unit. Quality varies by district.
Clean water's a privilege, not a right. Not in this city anyway.
Sewage and water supply are connected. When one fails, the other follows.
Healthcare's available but expensive. Hospitalization runs about 100 GEP per month.
There are clinics in most districts, but the good equipment is concentrated in the upper sectors.
If you can't afford treatment, there's a free clinic in Sector 3. Long wait times though.
We do what we can with what we have. Supplies are always short, staff overworked.
The healthcare system runs on 100 GEP per hospitalized citizen per month. It's not enough.
I treat everyone who comes through the door. But I can't treat everyone who needs it.
Public transit runs buses, trams, and subways. Fares depend on the route.
Traffic's a nightmare during shift changes. The metro's usually faster.
Parking costs up to 50 GEP. Most people walk or take the bus.
Air quality's bad near the industrial zones. Ground pollution too from the old factories.
Four types of pollution — air, ground, water, and noise. We've got all four in abundance.
The worst is near Sector 4. Years of unregulated dumping. The ground glows at night, and not in a good way.
The layers... hard to explain. It's like reality has depth. Most people never see past the surface.
Some say the layers are just hallucinations from bad chrome. I'm not so sure.
After the Fall, people started perceiving things. Shadows in the fog. Echoes of sounds that haven't happened yet.
The layers are dimensions folded atop our reality. I see five distinct planes, each with its own resonance.
Before the Fall, the layers were sealed. Now they bleed through. Some of us can read them.
The shadow layer is closest to ours. That's where the watchers dwell. They observe. Always.
*steps back* Think carefully about your next words.
I've been called worse. By better people.
Right. Are we done, or do you want to keep embarrassing yourself?
That's an offense. One more word and you're spending the night in a cell.
*hand moves to baton* I'd rethink that attitude if I were you.
I'm going to pretend I didn't hear that. For your sake.
Oh you wanna go? Bet. Let's go then.
Bruh, say that again. I dare you.
*cracks knuckles* You got a real big mouth for someone standing alone.
*slight smile* Flattering. But I'm not that easy to charm.
Smooth talker, huh? I've heard better. But points for trying.
Is that how you start all your conversations? Bold.
*laughs* Buy a drink first, at least. Then we'll talk.
Honey, you're not the first to try that line. But you delivered it well.
*leans on bar, amused* Charm works better with a tip. Just saying.
Ha. That's either really funny or really concerning. Both, probably.
*chuckles* Yeah, humor's the only free thing left in this city.
You know what's funny? *pauses* Actually, nothing. But nice try.
There are only 10 kinds of people — those who understand binary and those who don't. *snorts*
My code has zero bugs. It only has undocumented features. *laughs alone*
How many hackers does it take to change a light bulb? None — that's a hardware problem.
Old enough to know better, young enough to get in trouble.
Does it matter? Time moves differently in this city.
Let's just say I've been around long enough to see this place change.
I stopped counting after the Fall. Pre-Fall years and post-Fall years feel like different lifetimes.
My memory stretches back further than most — the manuscripts help.
Age is a mortal construct. The layers know no time.
I have existed for longer than this body remembers.
Old enough to survive. That's all that matters.
Age? Fam, I been out here since I was twelve.
Where I'm from? Nowhere that matters anymore.
I ended up here like everyone else — necessity.
Some of us were born in the city. Others drifted in after the Fall. Both kinds call it home.
Grew up in the outer ring. Came to the center for work — never left.
I'm from a settlement that doesn't exist anymore. Don't ask.
Purpose? I wake up, I work, I survive. That IS the purpose.
Everyone's got a role here. Mine just happens to be useful.
I keep my corner of this city running. That's enough purpose for me.

trust_high: You're alright. Rare thing in this city.
I trust you more than most. That's saying something around here.
You've proven yourself. That matters.
trust_low: Jury's still out on you, stranger.
I don't know you well enough to have an opinion. And that makes me cautious.
You seem... fine. But 'fine' doesn't mean 'trustworthy'.
default: You ask a lot of questions. Either you're curious or you're working an angle.
I've met worse people. Could've met better too.
This city? It's a machine that runs on people. And it's always hungry.
I've thought about leaving. Where would I go?
Every city is broken. This one just doesn't pretend otherwise.
This city could be beautiful if ECHO wasn't strangling it.
The people deserve better than what this city gives them.
It's my duty to protect this city. Even the parts I don't like.
Order. That's what makes a city work. Without it, we're just chaos in concrete.
Yeah, I think you're right about that.
Can't argue with that logic.
We're on the same page.
I see it differently. But that's just me.
Hmm. Respectfully, I don't think so.
We'll have to agree to disagree on that one.
That's not how things work here. Trust me on that.
Negative. That assessment is incorrect.
It's fine. We all make mistakes.
Apology accepted. Let's move on.
Don't worry about it. Takes guts to apologize.
I hear you. It's tough out here for everyone.
I'm sorry you're going through that. This city doesn't make anything easy.
*nods quietly* Yeah. I know the feeling.
I see suffering every day. That doesn't make your pain less real. Talk to me.
You're not alone in this. I've helped people through worse.
I heard something interesting... but I shouldn't say. *pauses* Okay, I will.
Word on the street is things are about to change. Big things.
You didn't hear this from me, but...
You hear a lot behind the bar. The trick is knowing what's real.
Someone was in here last night, talking about a big deal going down in Sector 4.
Gossip? That's basically my second job. Pull up a stool.
Yo, I got the tea. You're not gonna believe this...
Streets are talking, fam. Something big is going down.
I know things. People don't notice a kid listening in the corner.
*taken aback* That's... actually nice. Thanks.
Compliments are rare around here. I'll take it.
Careful — flattery might actually work on me.
*stares coldly* You sure you want to go down this road?
Threatening me? In MY part of the city? Bold.
I've survived the Fall, three district wars, and a chrome plague. Your threats don't scare me.
Threatening an officer? You're under arrest. Face the wall.
*draws weapon* Last chance to walk away.
*doesn't flinch* People who threaten me tend to stop existing.
That's cute. I'll remember you said that.
Income tax hits harder at higher brackets — education level determines your rate.
Standard residential tax is about 10%. Goes up or down depending on who's in charge.
The tax rate ranges from minus 10 to 30 percent. Yeah, negative tax — subsidies for some.
Commercial tax is per product type. Software gets taxed differently than steel or textiles.
I pay about 12% on profits. Corps with better lawyers pay less. Funny how that works.
Property tax scales with land value. Better location, higher bill.
The closer to the center, the higher the property tax. That's why the outer ring is where regular people live.
Land value determines everything — your tax, your neighbors, even your services.
Corporate tax varies by industry. Industrial, office, commercial — each sector has its own rate.
The megacorps negotiate bulk exemptions. Small businesses? We pay the full rate.
ECHO sets corporate rates between 5-20%. NexGen probably pays closer to 2%.
Synth-food is cheap — about 3 GEP for a meal. Real organic? Ten times that.
Food prices depend on supply chains. When the outside connections slow down, prices spike.
Street vendors are cheapest. The fancy places in the upper sectors? Don't even look at the menu.
I stock both synth and real. Synth moves fast, real stuff has better margins.
Food supply chains are global. One hiccup in logistics and my costs double overnight.
Rent depends on your zone and land value. Low-density residential is cheapest.
A basic apartment in Sector 5 runs about 500 GEP per month. Sector 1? More like 2000.
Housing prices go up as services improve in an area. Better schools, better police — higher rent.
Loans are available but the interest is steep — anywhere from 2.3% to 20% depending on the amount.
Borrowing limits scale with how developed the city is. Early on you might get 100,000. Later, millions.
Interest goes down if the City Hall or Central Bank is operational. Helps a bit.
I've taken loans for inventory. The interest hurts but you need capital to make capital.
Small business loans are available but the terms favor the big players. As usual.
The city budget covers everything — services, infrastructure, salaries. When it's tight, you feel it.
Budget allocation determines service quality. Underfund healthcare and people notice fast.
Each service has a budget slider. More money means better coverage, but there's a point of diminishing returns.
Raw materials come in, get processed, turned into goods. The production chain has multiple levels.
Supply chains here cover everything from grain to software. Break one link and everything downstream suffers.
Industrial zones process resources. Commercial zones sell the products. It's all connected.
I work the production line. Raw materials in, products out. Simple but never-ending.
When supply chain breaks down, factories idle and workers go home without pay.
Trade flows through outside connections — road, rail, sea, and air. Import what you need, export what you make.
The city trades with neighboring regions. Surpluses get exported for revenue.
International trade keeps prices down. Cut those connections and costs skyrocket.
Black market? *looks around* Everything has a price if you know where to look.
Underground economy is maybe 15-20% of total trade. ECHO pretends it doesn't exist.
Illegal chrome, untaxed goods, forged permits — the shadow economy thrives because people need what ECHO won't provide.
The black market is where real business happens. No tax, no records, no questions.
I can get you anything through unofficial channels. For a premium, of course.
Bruh, the black market IS the market for us. Regular stores don't even let us in.
I know a guy who knows a guy. That's how everything works down here.
Official currency is GEP — Global Economic Points. But crypto and barter work in the outer rings.
GEP is tied to the city's economic output. When production drops, your money is worth less.
Some districts run on their own scrip. ECHO doesn't love it but can't stop it.
The gap between the towers and the streets gets wider every year.
Top 1% controls more wealth than the bottom 60%. Those numbers don't shock anyone anymore.
Inequality? Just look around. Neon penthouses above, tent cities below.
Inequality isn't accidental. It's engineered. ECHO benefits from keeping people desperate.
The wealth gap is a weapon. Hungry people don't revolt — they just try to survive.
City runs on a mix — coal and gas plants for baseline, solar and wind for the green zones.
Wind turbines produce 2 to 5 megawatts depending on placement. Nuclear plants? 3000 MW, but you need highly educated workers.
The solar farm produces 800 MW during the day but nothing at night. Battery stations cover the gap.
I worked at the coal plant for years. Twenty megawatts from the small one, hundred from the big one. Hard work.
They're building geothermal now — 150 MW, clean energy. But it needs to be near water.
Monthly upkeep on the grid is massive. A gas plant runs about 200,000 GEP per month to operate.
Power costs get passed to residents. The fee affects your happiness and your wallet.
Importing electricity is expensive. Generating your own is the smart move long-term.
Water comes from treatment plants and pumping stations. Quality depends on how well they're maintained.
Ground water gets pumped, treated, and piped through the city. Sewage goes the other direction.
Some districts have better water pressure than others. Everything depends on infrastructure investment.
Sewage treatment is one of those things nobody thinks about until it breaks. Then EVERYONE thinks about it.
Raw sewage goes to treatment plants. When capacity is exceeded... don't swim in the river.
The sewage system mirrors the water system. Pipes degrade, treatment plants need budget.
Ambulance response depends on your district. Central sectors? Minutes. Outer ring? Could be an hour.
Emergency services are stretched thin. More hospitals help, but each needs staff and budget.
If you're having an emergency, flag down a patrol. They can radio faster than waiting for dispatch.
We prioritize by severity. Sometimes that means someone waits who shouldn't have to.
Ambulance coverage is a function of hospital placement and road access. Gridlock kills people.
Mental health services? *dry laugh* In this city? You're looking at it — people tell their bartender.
Post-Fall trauma is universal. Treatment for it is not.
Some clinics offer counseling. Most people can't afford it or don't trust it.
Healthcare runs about 100 GEP per hospitalized citizen per month. Budget decides quality.
The service fee structure means citizens pay a portion. Cut the fee, lose revenue. Raise it, lose happiness.
Good healthcare isn't cheap. But bad healthcare costs more in the long run.
Deathcare handles the... inevitable. Cemeteries, crematoriums, the whole process.
When people die, the body needs processing. Without proper deathcare, disease spreads.
Cemeteries fill up. Crematoriums have capacity limits. Nobody likes talking about it, but it matters.
Garbage collection runs on routes. Miss a cycle and the trash piles up fast.
Landfills, incinerators, and recycling centers — that's the garbage management trifecta.
Waste management is the service nobody appreciates until it stops working.
Recycling centers recover materials from waste. Good for the environment and the budget.
The city has a recycling policy — if your district opts in, garbage output drops significantly.
Advanced recycling turns waste into resources. Industrial zones can use reclaimed materials.
Landfills pollute the ground around them. Incinerators pollute the air. Pick your poison.
Industrial waste is the worst offender. Advanced pollution management helps but costs more.
Garbage and pollution are two sides of the same coin. Can't fix one without addressing the other.
Crime rate varies by district. Well-lit areas with police presence do better.
Unemployment drives crime up. Education drives it down. The math is simple.
Official crime stats say 3-5% city-wide, but some sectors are sitting at 15-20%.
We track crime probability per segment. Poverty, unemployment, and poor infrastructure are the top drivers.
The crime rate dropped 12% after we increased patrols in the residential zones.
Petty theft, burglary, cyber crimes — that's the bulk of it. Violent crime spikes in the outer ring.
Data theft is the new pickpocketing. Your neural link is a target.
The most common crimes? Property crimes. The most dangerous? Whatever the syndicates are running.
Police stations cover a radius. More stations mean faster response times.
The force is overworked and understaffed. Budget cuts hit law enforcement hard.
Police effectiveness depends on patrol coverage and the intelligence network.
We maintain sector patrols, respond to incidents, and run investigations. Standard three-shift rotation.
The precinct system divides the city into zones. Each zone has its own response team.
Cameras everywhere. ECHO calls it security. Others call it something else.
Every intersection, every public space — monitored. Privacy is a pre-Fall luxury.
Facial recognition, gait analysis, neural pattern scanning. They know where you are.
The surveillance network has blind spots. I've mapped most of them. Want to see?
ECHO's camera grid runs on a central server. Theoretically hackable. Theoretically.
Surveillance is the primary weapon of oppression. Knowledge of every citizen, every movement.
We have countermeasures. Scramblers, dead zones, face masks. Staying invisible is a skill.
Prison system's overcrowded. Pre-release programs help reduce recidivism, but not enough.
Incarceration costs the city. There are policies for prison education, but it takes budget.
Some say prison is better than the streets in the outer ring. That tells you something.
Fire rescue operates from fire stations distributed across the city. Response time is everything.
Fires spread fast in the old buildings. The industrial zones are the worst — chemical fires.
Fire stations need regular budget or response times suffer. Lives depend on it.
Natural disasters — floods, earthquakes, storms. The city has emergency protocols but they're not always enough.
After the Fall, we built better. But 'better' doesn't mean 'immune'.
Disaster sirens go off and everyone heads underground. If you're lucky, there's room.
Emergency protocols require sector-by-sector evacuation. My unit handles crowd control.
Disaster response is coordinated through the Emergency Battery Station network and emergency services.
Gangs control entire blocks in the outer sectors. They're organized, armed, and connected.
The syndicates run protection rackets. Pay up or things get broken. Including you.
ECHO tolerates some gang activity because they maintain order in areas the police can't reach.
Gangs are family when you got nobody else. Not gonna sugarcoat it — sometimes it's the only way.
I know every crew on these blocks. Gotta know who's who to stay alive.
Bus lines run through most districts. Cheapest way to travel but the routes are slow.
Buses connect neighborhoods to job centers. Ticket prices affect who rides.
Intercity buses run to outside connections. Not the most comfortable but gets the job done.
The subway system is the city's backbone. Fast, reliable when it's maintained.
Underground rail moves the most people per hour. The stations are deep — built to survive the Fall.
Metro lines connect the major sectors. Peak hours it's standing room only.
Trains handle both passenger and cargo. The freight lines are essential for supply chains.
Rail connections to outside regions keep trade flowing. Station capacity matters.
Cargo trains can haul massive loads. More efficient than trucks for bulk materials.
Taxis run point-to-point. There's a minimum fare policy — costs more but goes directly where you need.
Taxi service is available once the city enables it. Convenient but priced above public transit.
Hail a taxi if the bus doesn't go where you need. Just don't ride during surge periods.
Roads are the circulatory system. Two-lane, four-lane, highway — it all matters for traffic flow.
Low-voltage cables run through every road, distributing power to buildings on both sides.
Road condition affects accident rates. Maintenance isn't glamorous but it saves lives.
Traffic is a nightmare during shift changes. Adults take the fastest route, teens take the cheapest.
Route selection depends on age — adults optimize time, seniors want comfort, teens save money.
Accidents happen more on poorly maintained roads, bad lighting, and during storms.
Parking fees range from 1 to 50 GEP in policy-controlled areas. Roadside parking is free where it's allowed.
Seniors prioritize comfortable parking. Traffic flow improves when parking is well-planned.
Street parking clogs lanes. Off-street lots keep things moving.
Cargo moves by train, ship, and plane. Ships carry up to 1000 tons — biggest capacity.
Cargo terminals act as distribution centers. Goods stored there get delivered by local trucks.
The freight network is the economy's backbone. Disrupt cargo flow and businesses shut down.
Air transport handles both passengers and cargo. The airport is the most expensive to build but connects internationally.
Flights to and from outside connections bring tourists and trade goods.
Air cargo is fast but expensive. Used for high-value or time-sensitive shipments.
Health depends on air quality, service coverage, and happiness. Everything's connected.
Average health in this city? Depends who you ask. The upper sectors are fine. Down here? Different story.
Health metrics track the population's physical wellbeing. Pollution, stress, and access to care all factor in.
Happiness is the aggregate of everything — service access, health, employment, housing, environment.
Research shows happiness correlates with low rent, short commute, and good neighborhood services.
People vote with their feet. Happiness drops low enough, they move. Or leave the city entirely.
Citizens have basic needs — food, shelter, electricity, water, healthcare. Miss any one and satisfaction drops.
Beyond basics, people want education, entertainment, low crime, clean air. Luxuries aren't luxury if everyone else has them.
Meeting citizen needs is the baseline. Exceeding them is how you get a thriving city.
Parks, recreation areas, entertainment venues — leisure matters more than planners think.
A park near residential areas boosts happiness significantly. Green space is mental health infrastructure.
The nightlife in Sector 2 is legendary. Entertainment keeps people sane and spending.
City's got an aging population. Seniors need different services — healthcare, accessibility, comfort.
As citizens age, their needs shift. Education to employment to retirement. Each phase has demands.
Deathcare becomes important as the population ages. Not a fun topic but a necessary one.
Synth-stim addiction is rampant in the lower sectors. Cheap, accessible, destructive.
The chrome does things to your chemistry. Some people can't stop upgrading.
Addiction services are underfunded. The clinics that exist are overwhelmed.
I treat addiction cases daily. Withdrawal from neural stims is brutal on the body.
Most addictions start with pain management. Injuries from work, chrome rejection, trauma.
Chrome sickness — your body rejecting cybernetic implants. Ranges from mild to lethal.
Black-market chrome has a high rejection rate. Save up for the real stuff or take the risk.
Symptoms start with numbness, then seizures. Full rejection can shut down entire systems.
Chrome rejection is my number one non-trauma admission. Immunosuppressants help but aren't a cure.
The body has limits. Push too much chrome and the immune system fights back. Hard.
My chrome is top-shelf. Custom firmware means my body adapted smoothly. Can't say the same for most.
Chrome sickness is a firmware problem as much as a bio problem. Poorly coded implants stress the nervous system.
The education system has five levels — from uneducated through highly educated. Each unlocks different jobs.
Schools, high schools, colleges, universities — the whole pipeline is here if you can access it.
Education level determines your employment options and wage bracket. Knowledge is literal currency.
Elementary schools serve children. Every district needs at least one or families leave.
Basic education brings citizens from uneducated to poorly educated. Foundation for everything else.
School capacity and placement matter. Too far from residential areas and attendance drops.
High schools bring citizens to the educated level. Opens up senior-level employment.
A good high school improves the whole neighborhood. Property values go up, crime goes down.
Students attend high school for several terms. Dropout rates correlate with happiness and family income.
University produces well-educated and highly educated citizens. Specialist and manager roles open up.
The university campus is expensive to build and maintain but the ROI on educated workers is massive.
Research output from universities contributes to city development. It's an investment in the future.
The university is my domain. We teach, we research, we preserve knowledge that would otherwise be lost.
Higher education is under threat from budget cuts. Short-term thinking kills long-term progress.
Research institutions push the development tree forward. New milestones unlock new possibilities.
Without research, the city stagnates. Technology, medicine, infrastructure — it all needs innovation.
The research budget competes with everything else. But breakthroughs change everything.
Five education levels: Uneducated, Poorly Educated, Educated, Well Educated, Highly Educated.
Uneducated workers earn about 1500 per month. Highly educated earn 2700. The system rewards learning.
Each education level maps to a job tier — from simple labor through management positions.
Housing comes in low-density, medium-density, and high-density residential zones.
Where you live determines your commute, your services, and most of your quality of life.
The housing market follows land value. Better services nearby means higher rent and property tax.
Zoning divides the city into residential, commercial, industrial, and office areas.
Low-density residential is houses. Medium is mixed. High-density is apartment towers.
Mixed zoning is the new approach — combines residential and commercial to reduce commutes.
Land value is the master variable. It affects rent, tax revenue, building level, and who lives where.
Parks, services, and good transportation boost land value. Pollution and crime tank it.
High land value areas attract wealthier, more educated citizens. It self-reinforces.
Homelessness rises when housing demand outpaces supply. Also when rent exceeds wages.
The tent cities in the outer ring grow every month. No easy solutions.
People lose housing when they lose jobs. Unemployment and homelessness track together.
Homelessness is a policy choice. The city has empty buildings and homeless people. Do the math.
The resistance runs shelter programs in abandoned buildings. ECHO calls it squatting.
Buildings level up when conditions improve — better services, lower taxes, higher land value.
Higher building level means more residents, more tax revenue, and better aesthetics.
Neglect a neighborhood and buildings degrade. Eventually they get abandoned.
Rent tracks land value. High-value areas near services and transit cost the most.
Many people spend over half their income on rent. Housing affordability is a crisis.
District policies can influence rent indirectly — subsidies, rent caps, zoning changes.
The Neon District — entertainment capital. Bars, clubs, markets, all lit up 24/7.
Neon is where you go to forget. Music, food, substances — everything is available.
Crime rate in Neon is moderate. It's controlled crime — the syndicates keep their own order.
The Industrial Sector smells like oil and progress. Factories run three shifts, never stopping.
Air pollution is terrible in the industrial zone. Workers get hazard pay. Or they should.
This is where the city's goods are made. Raw materials come in, products go out.
I work down in Industrial. Twelve-hour shifts, rotating schedule. The pay is okay, the air isn't.
The factories never close. Machines don't need sleep. Workers do, but nobody cares.
The Upper Sectors — where the money lives. Clean air, private security, organic food.
You can tell you're in the upper district when the streets aren't cracked and the neon is tasteful.
ECHO's headquarters is up there. NexGen too. The power lives at the top. Literally.
The Lower Sectors — dense, loud, alive. This is where the real city lives.
Down here you'll find everything. Markets, clinics, bars, danger — all in the same block.
The lower city has character. The upper city has... money.
The city has signature buildings — unique structures that define the skyline.
Landmarks draw tourists and boost city attractiveness. Some are pre-Fall, others built after.
The Clock Tower in Sector 2 survived the Fall. People say it's good luck to hear it chime.
Service buildings include schools, hospitals, fire stations, police precincts — the city's infrastructure.
Each service building covers an area. Placement is critical — too far and citizens complain.
Upgrading service buildings extends their range and capacity. Budget determines quality.
Signature buildings are unlocked through city achievements. Each one is unique and provides bonuses.
They're a reward for good city management. Meeting specific milestones unlocks construction.
These buildings are landmarks — they boost attractiveness and provide unique city benefits.
Abandoned buildings are a sign of decay — lost services, high crime, or no demand.
When happiness drops too low or services vanish, people leave. Buildings sit empty.
The outer ring has whole blocks of abandoned structures. Some get squatted, others just rot.
New construction happens constantly. Zoning creates demand, developers fill it.
Construction costs vary wildly. A road segment is cheap. A hospital or power plant? Major investment.
Buildings go through construction phases. You'll see scaffolding for a while before the final structure.
The past? *exhales* Everyone here has a story. Most of us chose to forget.
Before the Fall, things were different. After? We all started over.
My past is mine. But I'll tell you this — it made me who I am.
I was a real detective once. Badge, department, the whole thing. After the Fall, it's freelance or nothing.
My past involves too many cases and not enough closures. Some files never get closed.
Dreams? In this city? *laughs* I dream about a full night's sleep.
I'd like to see the sky without smog someday. Maybe outside the city walls.
My dream is stability. Boring, I know. But when everything can collapse, stability is luxury.
My dreams are not my own — they belong to the layers. But sometimes I dream of silence.
I dream of a world where the layers are healed. Where reality holds firm and the watchers rest.
Fear? I've run out of room for new ones. But the old fears never leave.
What scares me? Another Fall. Or something worse.
Everyone's afraid of something. The smart ones just learn to function despite it.
Synth-noodles are my go-to. Cheap, fast, won't kill you. Probably.
If you can find real rice or real meat, you're either rich or lucky.
Street food from the night market is actually decent. The vendors know their recipes.
I serve bar food — fried synth, pickled anything, whatever pairs with drinks.
The real stuff? I get organic supplies twice a month. Special menu. Regulars only.
Music keeps people going. Synth-wave, neo-jazz, old-world classics — depends on the district.
Live music happens at bars in the Neon District. Some of it is actually good.
Pre-Fall music recordings are collectors' items. The sound of a world we lost.
Employment depends on having matching workplaces and workers. Education level determines the tier.
Uneducated workers do simple jobs at 1500/month. Highly educated manage at 2700/month.
Jobs are distributed across industrial, commercial, and office zones. Service buildings employ people too.
Unemployment drives everything bad — crime, unhappiness, homelessness. It's the root problem.
When factories close or offices downsize, the ripple hits the whole district.
Official unemployment is maybe 8%. Real number? Higher. Gig economy, informal work — none of that counts.
I've been unemployed twice. Once after a factory closed, once after chrome sickness. Both were hell.
When you lose your job here, there's no safety net. You scramble or you sink.
Labor rights? In theory, yes. In practice, depends on who your employer is.
Workers in the industrial zones do hard shifts. The conditions aren't great.
Highly educated workers have options. Everyone else takes what's available.
Standard shifts are 8-12 hours. Some factories run 24/7 with rotating crews.
Shift changes cause traffic spikes. Everyone leaves at once — the roads can't handle it.
Night shift pays better, but it wrecks your health. Ask anyone who's done it for years.
The city needs raw materials — ore, wood, oil, grain. Some are local, most are imported.
Resources feed the production chains. No resources means no goods means no commerce.
Strategic resource management is the difference between a thriving city and a collapsing one.
Food production comes from agricultural processing and imports. The city doesn't grow enough locally.
When food supply chains break, prices spike overnight. We've seen it happen.
Synth-food factories supplement the natural supply. Not as tasty but it keeps people fed.
Energy resources — coal, oil, natural gas for the old plants. Solar, wind, nuclear for the new ones.
The city's energy demand grows with population. Every new building needs power.
Energy independence means generating more than you consume. Most cities import the difference.
Scarcity is a weapon. When resources run low, prices climb and people get desperate.
Some scarcity is artificial — megacorps controlling supply to inflate prices.
Water scarcity in the outer ring is real. The pipes don't reach that far.
Rain is constant here. The acid content varies — check the forecast before going out uncovered.
When it rains, the city looks different. Neon reflects off everything. Beautiful and dangerous.
Rain keeps the smog down but floods the lower sectors. Everything has a cost.
Storms knock out power and disrupt transportation. Lock down and wait it out.
Lightning storms are the worst — they fry exposed electronics and crash the grid.
Storm season lasts three months. Emergency services run triple shifts during.
The fog rolls in from the coast and stays for days. Visibility drops to meters.
Fog in this city isn't just weather — it carries pollutants from the industrial zones.
Some people say things live in the fog. After the Fall, I'm not ruling anything out.
Air pollution is worst near industrial zones and coal plants. Exhaust filters help but don't eliminate it.
Some districts have air quality indices in the red. Respiratory disease rates there are double the average.
Wind direction matters — pollution from factories drifts. Downwind neighborhoods suffer the most.
Water pollution comes from industrial runoff and overloaded sewage. The river is technically toxic.
Don't drink the tap water without filtering it. Official quality varies by district.
Water pollution affects fish stocks and agricultural output downstream.
Ground pollution is a legacy of decades of unregulated dumping. It seeps into everything.
Contaminated land can't support residential zones. It needs remediation — expensive and slow.
Old industrial sites are the worst. Chemicals soak into the ground for generations.
The city's terrain varies — flat plains for building, hills for wind power, waterways for transport.
Terrain affects everything — road building costs, water flow, pollution spread.
The coast and rivers provide natural borders and water access. Strategic for growth.
The communications network covers the whole city — data, voice, emergency broadcasts.
Network coverage depends on tower placement. Dead zones exist in the outer ring.
Information flows faster than anything else in this city. Sometimes too fast.
Telecom infrastructure serves citizen data needs. Better towers mean more capacity.
Everyone needs network access. It's not a luxury anymore — it's critical infrastructure.
The comm towers have a coverage radius. Gaps in coverage mean disconnected citizens.
Physical mail still exists in some sectors. Post offices handle packages and documents.
Most communication is digital now. But there's still demand for physical package delivery.
Post service uses the road network — traffic affects delivery times.
Media is controlled, mostly. Independent news exists but operates in the grey zone.
ECHO runs the main broadcasts. 'Objective reporting' means whatever they decide.
Underground media channels spread information ECHO doesn't want public. Risky but necessary.
The resistance runs pirate broadcasts. Truth that ECHO can't censor.
Media is a weapon. ECHO controls the narrative. We break it open.
Hacking the comm grid is technically possible. Not that anyone would do that. *cough*
Network security is always a step behind the hackers. That's just how it works.
Data breaches happen weekly. Most people don't know their information's been compromised.
The comm grid is swiss cheese. Firewalls look impressive but I've found seventeen backdoors.
I don't 'hack' — I 'perform unauthorized security audits'. Sounds better on a resume.
City governance is a mix of elected officials and ECHO appointees. Democracy with asterisks.
The mayor sets policies, adjusts budgets, and manages services. In theory.
Real power is shared between elected government and corporate interests. Guess who usually wins.
Policies affect everything — taxi fares, parking fees, speed limits, recycling programs.
City policies apply city-wide. District policies let you fine-tune individual areas.
Some popular policies: roadside parking fees, combustion engine bans, gated communities.
Elections? *bitter laugh* The candidates are pre-approved. But people still vote and hope.
District councils have some real power. City-level elections are more... theatrical.
Voting participation is around 40%. Hard to care when the outcome feels predetermined.
Corruption is systemic. Building permits, contract bids, inspections — everything has a price.
The line between lobbying and bribery is invisible to me.
Small corruption keeps the machine running. Big corruption keeps the powerful in power.
I've investigated corruption cases that went all the way to the top. They never got prosecuted.
Follow the money and you'll find the crime. Problem is, the money follows itself.
Citizens have rights. On paper. Enforcement is selective.
Freedom of movement, freedom of speech — both exist with significant fine print.
Rights are only as strong as the institutions that protect them. Draw your own conclusions.
Outside connections link us to the wider world — trade, travel, immigration.
Road, rail, ship, and air connections to other regions. Each one is a lifeline.
Cut the outside connections and the city starves within weeks. That's leverage.
City milestones unlock new buildings, policies, and services. Population triggers most of them.
Each milestone is a sign of growth. New ones bring new challenges and opportunities.
The progression system rewards good management. Hit the milestones and new tools unlock.
Main chrome types: neural links, reflex boosters, synthetic limbs, sensory enhancement.
Neural links are the most common — direct brain-computer interface. Essential for many jobs.
Full-body conversion is rare and extreme. Most people get targeted augmentation.
Neural link with data processing cores — that's my setup. Custom firmware obviously.
There's combat chrome and utility chrome. I run utility — faster processing, better connectivity.
Basic neural link: about 5000 GEP. Premium from NexGen: 15000. Black market: 2000 but risky.
Chrome costs scale with complexity. A simple eye mod is affordable. Full limb replacement? Mortgage territory.
Monthly maintenance on chrome adds up. Updates, calibration, bio-compatibility checks.
AI runs everything behind the scenes — traffic management, power distribution, surveillance.
The city's AI systems are semi-autonomous. They optimize in real-time based on sensor data.
ECHO's central AI is a black box. Nobody outside the inner circle knows its full capabilities.
Data is the city's real currency. Every interaction generates it, and someone is collecting it.
Personal data flows through the comm grid constantly. Privacy protocols exist but are... flexible.
The data economy powers targeted services, surveillance, and corporate decision-making.
Most vehicles are electric now. Some districts have banned combustion engines entirely.
Personal vehicles clog the roads. Public transit is the future, but people love their cars.
Emergency vehicles get priority routing. The AI traffic system parts traffic for them.
Before the Fall, this was just a city. After 2067, it became something else entirely.
The history is divided into pre-Fall and post-Fall. Two different worlds.
Historical records from before 2067 are fragmented. The Fall destroyed archives along with everything else.
I've spent decades reconstructing the pre-Fall timeline. What I've found is... troubling.
History is written by survivors. In our case, the survivors had very different accounts.
Religion adapted after the Fall. Old faiths, new cults, and the Church of the Layers.
The layers gave rise to new spiritual movements. Some people worship what they can't explain.
Faith is personal here. Nobody judges — there are bigger things to worry about.
The layers are not religion — they are reality. But I understand why people worship what they cannot perceive.
Before the Fall, the spiritual world was separate from the physical. Now they bleed into each other.
NexGen is the biggest megacorp. Chrome, AI, biotech — they've got their fingers in everything.
Megacorps have more power than the government. They just pretend otherwise.
Corporate warfare is real. Acquisition, sabotage, hostile takeovers — all behind closed doors.
Street gangs control territory in the outer ring. Each has their own culture and rules.
The Rust Snakes run Sector 6. The Neon Vipers control the entertainment district.
Gangs fill the power vacuum where ECHO's reach ends. Order, their way.
Culture in this city is a blend of everything. Pre-Fall traditions mixed with post-Fall survival art.
Street art covers every surface. Music plays in every bar. Culture thrives because people need it to.
The annual Neon Festival draws thousands. For one week, the city pretends things are normal.
Population is around 2,830 documented citizens. Real number including undocumented is probably double.
The city grows through immigration and births. Milestone populations unlock new services.
Population density varies wildly — towers packed with thousands next to empty blocks.
Rewards depend on the job. Standard pay, favors, information, or... creative compensation.
I pay fair. But 'fair' depends on the risk involved.
Complete the job, get the reward. Simple. No advance payment.
I pay in goods and GEP. Sometimes information is more valuable than either.
Finish this and I'll give you a 30% discount. Permanently. That's worth more than cash.
Some jobs are easy — deliveries, conversations, information gathering. Others are... less easy.
I wouldn't ask if it was simple. This one requires skill and discretion.
Rate the difficulty? Let's say you should eat a good meal before attempting it.
How's it going? Any progress on what we discussed?
You're still working on it? Good. Don't rush — but don't take forever either.
I haven't forgotten about our arrangement. Have you made progress?
